name: The Tale of Kieu (Truyện Kiều)
blurb: Nguyễn Du's verse novel of a gifted young woman who sells herself to save her family
title: The Tale of Kieu (Truyện Kiều) Summary: Plot and Characters
description: Truyện Kiều by Nguyễn Du explained: the main characters, a plot summary of Thúy Kiều's fifteen years of suffering, the ending and the key themes.
h1: The Tale of Kieu (Truyện Kiều): Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Truyện Kiều, also called Đoạn trường tân thanh (A New Cry from a Broken Heart), is a Vietnamese verse novel by Nguyễn Du (1765–1820), written in Nôm script in 3,254 lines of lục bát (six-eight) verse. It retells a Chinese prose romance set in Ming-dynasty China. The heroine, Thúy Kiều, is beautiful and talented, and the poem follows how she gives up her first love and sells herself to save her father and brother. It is the best-known work of Vietnamese literature and is studied in every Vietnamese school.

body: Other figures include Đạm Tiên, a singer who died young and whose grave Kiều visits; Giác Duyên, a Buddhist nun; and Hồ Tôn Hiến, a Ming governor.

Part one: meeting and separation. During the Thanh minh festival, Thúy Kiều, Thúy Vân and their brother Vương Quan pass the neglected grave of Đạm Tiên, a famous singer who died young and alone. Kiều weeps for her and writes a poem; she feels that beauty and talent bring a harsh fate. On the same outing she meets Kim Trọng, a scholar who later rents a room next to the Vương house. The two meet in secret, exchange keepsakes and swear to marry. Kim Trọng is then called away to Liêu Dương to mourn his uncle.

While he is gone, a silk merchant falsely accuses Kiều's father, and officials arrest him and Vương Quan. To pay for their release, Kiều sells herself in marriage. Before she leaves, she asks Thúy Vân to marry Kim Trọng in her place.

Part two: years of suffering. The buyer, Mã Giám Sinh, pays four hundred taels and takes Kiều away, but he works for Tú Bà, a brothel keeper. Kiều tries to kill herself and survives. Tú Bà shuts her up in the tower of Ngưng Bích, where she longs for her parents and Kim Trọng. Sở Khanh promises to rescue her, runs off once they flee, and Tú Bà catches and beats her until she gives in and works as a courtesan.

Thúc Sinh buys her freedom and makes her his second wife. His father objects and takes the matter to court, but the magistrate admires a poem Kiều writes and lets the marriage stand. Thúc Sinh's first wife, Hoạn Thư, finds out. While he is away she has Kiều kidnapped, renames her Hoa Nô and makes her a servant in her own house, then forces her to play music for Thúc Sinh in front of her. Kiều is later sent to copy sutras in a small Buddhist shrine, then escapes. The nun Giác Duyên takes her in but, fearing trouble, sends her to a woman called Bạc Bà, who sells her into another brothel through Bạc Hạnh.

Part three: Từ Hải and the return. The rebel Từ Hải meets Kiều, buys her freedom and marries her. When his army wins, he lets her sit in judgement: she repays everyone who helped her, including Thúc Sinh and Giác Duyên, and has those who wronged her punished, among them Tú Bà, Mã Giám Sinh, Sở Khanh, Bạc Bà and Bạc Hạnh. She spares Hoạn Thư, who admits her fault and argues that jealousy is only human.

The governor Hồ Tôn Hiến sends envoys and gifts offering peace. Kiều, hoping for a safe life and a way home, persuades Từ Hải to surrender. It is a trap: his army is ambushed and Từ Hải dies on his feet. Hồ Tôn Hiến makes Kiều play at his feast and then gives her to a local chief. On the boat, crossing the Tiền Đường river, she remembers Đạm Tiên's prophecy in a dream and throws herself into the water. Giác Duyên, waiting there, has her pulled out, and Kiều lives with the nun as a Buddhist recluse.

Kim Trọng returns, learns what happened and marries Thúy Vân as Kiều asked, but he never stops looking for her. He and Vương Quan pass the examinations and become officials. After hearing that Kiều drowned in the Tiền Đường river, the family goes there to hold a funeral rite and meets Giác Duyên, who tells them she is alive. Fifteen years after she left home, Kiều is reunited with her parents, siblings and Kim Trọng.

Thúy Vân urges her sister to marry Kim Trọng. Kiều agrees to live with them but refuses to be his wife in body, because she feels she can no longer offer him the purity of her youth. They live together as companions in poetry and music. The poem ends with Nguyễn Du's reflection that fate is set by Heaven, that talent and destiny are at odds, and that a good heart matters more than talent.

Readers have taken this ending in several ways. The most common school reading is Buddhist and moral: Kiều's suffering pays off a debt of fate (nghiệp), and her loyalty and filial sacrifice finally bring peace. A second reading stresses humanist protest: Nguyễn Du shows a society where money and power crush a gifted woman, and his sympathy is with her, not with the order that hurt her. Some critics also read the poem as an allegory of Nguyễn Du's own life, a man who served the new Nguyễn dynasty while his loyalty stayed with the fallen Lê, much as Kiều yields to circumstance while her heart stays with Kim Trọng. Which reading fits best is debated.

ul: Talent and fate: the poem returns again and again to the idea that great beauty and gifts invite misfortune, from Đạm Tiên's grave to Kiều's own life.
Filial duty and sacrifice: Kiều gives up her love and her body to save her father, which Vietnamese readers have long treated as the heart of her virtue.
Money and power: officials, brothel keepers and traders treat Kiều as goods to be bought and resold, and bribery decides her family's case.
Love and loyalty: Kiều's promise to Kim Trọng survives fifteen years, and the ending turns it into a lasting bond without marriage.
Compassion for the powerless: the narrator's voice keeps taking the side of a woman with no control over her fate, which is why the poem is called humanist.

Form and length: 3,254 lines in lục bát, the Vietnamese six-eight metre, originally written in Nôm script and now read in the modern Latin alphabet (chữ Quốc ngữ); the plot covers about fifteen years.

Source: Nguyễn Du adapted the Chinese prose novel Kim Vân Kiều truyện by an author known as Thanh Tâm Tài Nhân. He kept the plot but cut and reordered it and added the lyrical passages that made the poem famous.

Translations and adaptations: English versions include Huỳnh Sanh Thông's The Tale of Kieu (1983) and Timothy Allen's The Song of Kieu (2019); the story has been staged in cải lương and chèo and filmed several times, from 1924 to 2021.
Content: the plot involves human trafficking, forced prostitution, beatings and attempted suicide, told in a restrained, poetic way.

What teachers usually ask about: the portraits of Thúy Vân and Thúy Kiều, Kiều alone in the tower of Ngưng Bích, the theme of talent versus fate, Nguyễn Du's humanist view, and the poem's use of folk language and imagery.

check.q: Why does Kiều sell herself at the start of her ordeal?
options: To free her father and brother after a false accusation
To pay for Kim Trọng's studies
To escape a marriage arranged by Tú Bà
check.why: A silk merchant's false charge gets her father and Vương Quan arrested, and the money from her sale buys their release.

check.q: Who persuades Từ Hải to surrender to the governor Hồ Tôn Hiến?
check.why: Kiều trusts the governor's offer of peace and talks Từ Hải into surrendering, which leads to his death.

check.q: How does the poem end for Kiều and Kim Trọng?
options: Kiều dies in the Tiền Đường river
They live together as companions in poetry and music, not as husband and wife
check.why: Reunited after fifteen years, Kiều refuses a physical marriage and keeps Kim Trọng's love as friendship.

faq.q: Why is Truyện Kiều also called Đoạn trường tân thanh?
faq.a: Đoạn trường tân thanh, A New Cry from a Broken Heart, is the title Nguyễn Du gave the poem; Truyện Kiều, the Story of Kiều, is the popular name used today.

faq.q: Is Truyện Kiều based on a Chinese story?
faq.a: Yes. It adapts the Chinese prose romance Kim Vân Kiều truyện by Thanh Tâm Tài Nhân, set in Ming China; the plot is borrowed, but the verse, the imagery and the narrator's sympathy are Nguyễn Du's own.

faq.q: Why did Kiều forgive Hoạn Thư?
faq.a: When Kiều judges her enemies, Hoạn Thư admits her wrongs, reminds Kiều that she once let her leave and says jealousy is ordinary for a wife, and Kiều accepts this and lets her go.
